title: What Happens If You Sneeze With Your Eyes Open?
sources: Cleveland Clinic, 'Sneezing' (sneezing is an involuntary burst of air forced from your lungs through your nose and mouth; closing your eyes when you sneeze is an automatic reflex reaction; it's possible to sneeze with your eyes open, but it takes a lot of concentration to override the natural response, and your eyes won't pop out if you do): https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/sneezing

Texas A&M University news release via ScienceDaily, 'Can you sneeze with your eyes open?', 2016-12-09 (allergist David Huston, MD: 'absolutely possible' to sneeze without closing the eyes; the eye-closing reflex is likely protective, keeping more irritants out of the eyes, though there is no definitive data; the eyeball myth traces to an April 1882 New York Times story of a woman on a street car who was 'seized with a sudden fit of sneezing' and 'burst one of her eyeballs', called a far-fetched tale with little to no evidence; pressure from a sneeze is 'extremely unlikely' to pop an eyeball out, even with eyes open): https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/12/161209081007.htm

Cleveland Clinic, 'Eye Muscles' (both of your eyes have six muscles that control movement, four rectus and two oblique; they attach to the outside of your eyeball): https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/eye-muscles

Tease (next video): Guinness World Records, 'Highest equivalent altitude exposure survived' (Jim LeBlanc, a NASA volunteer testing space suits, 14 December 1966, Houston depressurisation chamber, equivalent of 120,000 ft after a hose disconnected; he recalled feeling his own saliva boiling off his tongue just before he lost consciousness; no long-term effects): https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/447311-highest-equivalent-altitude-exposure-survived
